newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Korea's Daewoo in Sri Lanka "national car" venture.
newsitem.headline: Korea's Daewoo in Sri Lanka "national car" venture.

text.p: South Korea's Daewoo Group is considering investing in an automobile assembly plant in Sri Lanka, chairman of the Board of Investment (BOI) Thilan Wijesinghe said on Saturday.
"Daewoo is seriously considering the setting up of an export-oriented automobile plant in Sri Lanka," Wijesinghe told a news conference.

Wijesinghe said Daewoo's group chairman Kim Woo-choong was at present visiting the Indian Ocean island to assess its engineering and manufacturing capability to source various components for the automobile industry.

"The Daewoo delegation is mindful of the fact that our domestic market for automobiles is relatively small. However, the company's strategy is to form certain alliances with Daewoo's investment in an automobile plant in India," he said.
He added the visiting delegation was convinced Sri Lanka was suitable for a plant with a capacity of about 80,000 to 100,000 cars per year, of which around 90 percent would be exported.
Officials for Daewoo Motors (India Ltd) recently said the company expected to produce 32,000 cars in 1997/98, up from 17,000 in the previous year.
South Korea's Daewoo Corporation holds a 91.6 percent stake in the company.
Wijesinghe said Daewoo Group chairman Kim Woo-choong had come to Sri Lanka after initial fact-finding was completed by senior company officials who have visited the island many times before.
"It is more than a goodwill visit. It is really to further cement business opportunities. He was very focused as to what he wanted to discuss," he said.
Sri Lanka has actively wooed South Korean investment after an official visit to that country by President Chandrika Kumaratunga last August.
Ninety three South Korean companies have already invested more than $300 million in Sri Lanka, becoming the island's number one source of foreign direct investment, Wijesinghe said.
In October last year, Korea Heavy Industries and Construction Co Ltd (Hanjung) bought 90 percent of the government-owned Ceylon Steel Corporation for $15 million.
Korea Heavy also hopes to invest $150 million in a power plant and $350 million in an oil refinery under a long-term investment plan.
Wijesinghe said the Daewoo chief "has assured to us that he will submit his proposal for the automobile plant by end of June".
"The chairman of Daewoo is also keen that the automobile plant should have the status of a national car, which many Asian countries have used as a strategy for industrialisation," Wijesinghe said.
He said Daewoo was also studying a proposal to set up a financial services company in Sri Lanka which will engage in activities such as commercial banking, leasing, insurance and consumer credit.
"The chairman of Daewoo felt that the presence of a very capitalised Korean financial institution is absolutely vital if Sri Lanka is to attract more large scale Korean investment," he said.
